prompt: What problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve that HTTP/1.1 keep-alive does not?

options.text: HTTP/2 encrypts every request by default, while HTTP/1.1 keep-alive sends traffic in plaintext
HTTP/2 runs many request–response streams at once on one connection, without waiting in turn
HTTP/2 switches the transport from TCP to UDP, so one lost packet never stalls the connection
HTTP/2 compresses response bodies automatically, which HTTP/1.1 keep-alive cannot do at all

explanation: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses a connection but still processes one request at a time (serial). HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent streams on one connection. (a) Both versions can use TLS; encryption is not what multiplexing adds. (c) HTTP/2 still uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. (d) Both versions support body compression via Content-Encoding; HTTP/2 adds header compression, not body compression.

prompt: Why does HTTP/3 use QUIC (over UDP) instead of TCP?

options.text: UDP is more reliable than TCP on lossy links, so QUIC can skip its own retransmissions
QUIC provides per-stream reliability, eliminating TCP-level head-of-line blocking
TCP cannot carry TLS-encrypted traffic, so encrypted HTTP needed a new transport
UDP is required for binary framing, which HTTP/3 needs and TCP's byte stream cannot carry

explanation: TCP enforces ordering across the entire connection; one lost packet blocks all streams. QUIC handles reliability per stream, so a loss on one stream does not affect others. (a) UDP itself is unreliable; QUIC adds its own retransmission on top. (c) TCP carries TLS just fine; that is how HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 works. (d) There is no such requirement: HTTP/2 already uses binary framing over TCP.

prompt: Which HTTP method is both **safe** and **idempotent**?

options.text: POST
PUT
GET
DELETE

explanation: GET does not change server state (safe) and repeating it gives the same result (idempotent). (a) POST is neither safe nor idempotent. (b) PUT is idempotent but not safe (it changes the resource). (d) DELETE is idempotent but not safe.

prompt: What does it mean for PUT to be **idempotent**?

options.text: PUT requests always succeed, so a client never has to check the response status code
Sending the same PUT request multiple times has the same effect as sending it once
PUT requests never change server state, so repeating them can never cause side effects
PUT responses can never be cached, so every repeat goes all the way to the origin server

explanation: Idempotent means the result is the same whether you send the request once or many times. The first PUT sets the resource; subsequent identical PUTs set it to the same value. (a) PUT can fail with 4xx or 5xx. (c) PUT does change state; that makes it unsafe, while idempotency is about repeats having the same effect. (d) Cacheability is separate from idempotency.

prompt: A client receives a `304 Not Modified` response. What does this mean?

options.text: The resource does not exist at this URL anymore, so the client should drop its copy
The resource has not changed since the client's last request; use the cached version
The server hit an error and could not build a fresh response, so it sent no body
The resource moved to the URL in the Location header, so the client should follow it

explanation: 304 is returned when a conditional request (If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since) shows the content has not changed. The server sends no body, saving bandwidth. (a) That is 404 (or 410). (c) Server errors are 5xx. (d) Redirects are 3xx but specifically 301, 302, 307, 308; 304 carries no new location.

prompt: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Cache-Control: no-store`?

options.text: They are identical; both tell every cache to keep no copy of the response at all
no-cache stores the response but revalidates before each use; no-store never stores it
no-cache forbids storing the response; no-store stores it but revalidates before each use
no-cache applies only to browser caches; no-store applies only to shared caches like CDNs

explanation: no-cache stores the response but requires the client to check with the origin before using it (via conditional request). no-store means do not store the response at all. (a) is the common misreading of no-cache as 'don't cache'. (c) swaps the two meanings. (d) Both directives apply to any cache, private or shared.

scenario: Your API has a POST /orders endpoint. A client sends an order but gets a network timeout and does not know if the server received it.
prompt: How should the system handle retries safely?

options.text: Retry the same POST blindly; an occasional duplicate order is cheaper than any extra server logic
Send an idempotency key with each request; the server returns the stored response for a seen key
Switch the endpoint from POST to GET, since GET is idempotent and can be retried without harm
Never retry automatically; show an error and make the user re-enter the whole order from scratch

explanation: An idempotency key lets the server detect duplicate requests and return the same response without processing the order twice. (a) Duplicate orders mean double charges and double deliveries, a real business problem. (c) GET must be safe; using it to create orders breaks HTTP semantics, and caches or prefetchers could trigger it. (d) is poor user experience and does not solve the issue: the user's re-entry is itself a retry that can duplicate the order.

scenario: A front-end team deploys a new version of their JavaScript bundle. The old bundle is cached by browsers and a CDN with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400`. Users still see the old version.
prompt: What caching strategy would prevent this problem?

options.text: Serve every JavaScript file with Cache-Control: no-store so browsers and the CDN never keep a copy
Put a content hash in the filename (app.3f8a.js), cache it a year as immutable, update the HTML
Set max-age=0 on the bundle so every request goes back to the origin and always gets the latest
Purge the CDN after each deploy, which also forces browsers to re-fetch the bundle on next load

explanation: Content-hashed filenames change when the code changes, so the browser requests the new URL (cache miss) and caches it for a long time. The HTML page (served with a short max-age or no-cache) references the new filename. (a) and (c) eliminate caching entirely, increasing load and latency. (d) A CDN purge does not reach browser caches: browsers keep their copy until their own max-age of 86400 runs out.

scenario: An API returns user profile data. The profile changes infrequently (maybe once a month). You want browsers to cache it but not serve stale data after an update.

options.text: public, max-age=2592000 (30 days), since the profile only changes about once a month anyway
private, no-cache with an ETag: the browser stores it but revalidates each use, 304 if unchanged
no-store, so the browser downloads a fresh copy on every view and can never show a stale profile
public, s-maxage=2592000, so the CDN holds it for 30 days while browsers fetch it every time

explanation: private keeps user data out of shared caches (CDNs). no-cache with ETag revalidation ensures the browser always checks for updates, but avoids re-downloading the body when nothing changed (304). (a) and (d) are public and could leak user data through shared caches; also, a 30-day lifetime serves stale data after an update. (c) is fresh but wastes bandwidth by always re-downloading, and it does not cache at all, which the requirement asked for.

prompt: Which of the following HTTP methods are **idempotent**? Select all that apply.

options.text: GET
POST
PUT
DELETE

explanation: GET, PUT and DELETE are all idempotent: repeating them produces the same result. POST is not idempotent: repeating it may create multiple resources. (b) is the exception because each POST can have a different side effect.
